passage: In the Andheri flat, Leela had been rubbing out the same letter in her Hindi copy for ten minutes. Rub, write, rub. Suddenly the page ripped, a jagged hole right through her homework. She burst into tears. "Now it's ruined! I can't take it to school like this. Ma'am will think I'm careless." Her mother, Vinita, put down the vegetables and sat beside her. Leela's shoulders were shaking. "It was only one letter," Vinita said softly. "Remember when you learnt to swim? You swallowed so much water first." Leela sniffed. "That's different." "Is it? Mistakes are how you learnt." Leela stared at the torn page, hiccupping, not yet convinced.

qa.q: How long had Leela been rubbing out the same letter?
qa.a: For ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Leela afraid of when the page ripped?
qa.a: She was scared that the torn page meant failure and that Ma'am would think she was careless.

qa.q: How could Vinita keep helping Leela with mistakes?
qa.a: Keep reminding her gently that mistakes are how learning works, like swimming, and let her hand in imperfect work.

qa.q: What is it like for Vinita to see Leela cry over one letter?
qa.a: Vinita likely feels worried and tender, seeing how much a tiny error hurts her daughter.

grounding: Shows a child who rubs out work until it tears and cries at a small error, and a parent saying mistakes are how learning happens.

passage:
"Asif, time to hand in the drawings."
"I can't, Madhav-sir. The sun is wrong."
"The sun looks lovely."
"It's not round. One side is flat. I'll do it again at home."
"You've started this one four times today. Look, the paper's gone thin."
Asif's chin wobbled. "If it's not perfect, it's bad."
"Can I show you something?" Madhav-sir opened his own sketchbook. "This horse. I drew the legs wrong three times. See the smudges?"
"But you're a teacher."
"Teachers learn by making mistakes too. That's how the legs got better."
Asif looked at the flat sun. A tear dripped onto the paper. "Can I hand it in with a note that says 'sun wrong'?"
"You can. I'd love to see it."

qa.q: How many times had Asif started the drawing that day?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: Why did Asif's chin wobble?
qa.a: He felt upset and afraid, believing that any flaw made his drawing bad.

qa.q: What did Madhav-sir do that helped Asif?
qa.a: He showed his own smudged horse and said teachers learn by making mistakes too.

qa.q: What might Madhav-sir be thinking when Asif asks to add a note?
qa.a: He is probably relieved and pleased that Asif is willing to hand in imperfect work.

grounding: Illustrates a child who restarts work and refuses to hand it in unless perfect, helped by a teacher who shares his own mistakes.

passage: Last year I cried over a spelling test where I got nine out of ten. Zubin got six and was cheerful all day. I didn't understand how. I'm Madhav, and I used to rub things out so many times my notebooks had holes. I wouldn't hand in my science project because one label was crooked, and Ma'am gave me a zero for not handing it in, which was worse than crooked. Then Zubin showed me his cricket bat, full of dents. "Every dent is a ball I missed," he said, "and now I hit them." That stuck with me. I still hate mistakes. But now I hand things in, even crooked ones.

qa.q: What score did Madhav get on the spelling test?
qa.a: Nine out of ten.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel about the crooked label?
qa.a: Madhav felt that one flaw meant failure, so the project felt too shameful to hand in.

qa.q: What lesson helped Madhav change?
qa.a: Zubin's dented bat showed that misses are how you learn to hit, so Madhav started handing work in.

qa.q: How might Zubin see his six out of ten?
qa.a: Zubin seems relaxed and cheerful about it, treating mistakes as part of getting better.

grounding: Shows a child who cried over small errors and refused to hand in imperfect work, learning that mistakes are part of learning.

passage: At the parent-teacher meeting in the school hall, Kishore listened as the class teacher praised his son Anand's neat notebooks, top marks and perfect attendance. Kishore felt the old swell of pride. Then she added quietly, "He cried in class on Monday because he wrote one answer in the wrong box. He wouldn't stop until I let him redo the whole page." Kishore's pride turned into a knot. On the way to the car, Anand walked a step behind, silent. Kishore stopped under the neem tree. "You know, at my first job I sent a letter to the wrong company. My boss laughed, and I fixed it. I was fine." Anand looked up. "You never told me that." "Your high standards are great. Mistakes are allowed too."

qa.q: Why did Anand cry in class on Monday?
qa.a: He wrote one answer in the wrong box.

qa.q: What did Kishore feel during the meeting?
qa.a: He felt torn: proud of Anand's work, then worried when he heard about the crying.

qa.q: Which choice of Kishore's was wise, and why?
qa.a: Sharing his own work mistake without shaming Anand's standards, which showed that errors can be fixed.

qa.q: How might Anand feel hearing about the wrong letter?
qa.a: Anand is likely surprised and a little relieved to learn his father made mistakes too.

grounding: Shows a parent torn between pride and worry about a perfectionist child, sharing his own mistake without shaming high standards.

passage:
Monday: Vijay tore up his maths worksheet because one sum had a crossing-out, and sobbed at the dining table. Charu felt proud of how much he cared, and scared by how hard he cried.
Wednesday: While frying puris, Charu burnt the first batch. "Oops, burnt them all," she said, laughing. "First batch is always practice." Vijay stared at her.
Saturday: Vijay handed her his English homework with one word scratched out. "It's good enough," he said, sounding unsure. Charu didn't praise the neatness. She said, "I like how you kept going." He smiled a little.

qa.q: What did Charu burn on Wednesday?
qa.a: The first batch of puris.

qa.q: What did Charu feel on Monday when Vijay tore up the worksheet?
qa.a: She felt proud of how much he cared and scared by how hard he cried.

qa.q: What worked in how Charu helped Vijay over the week?
qa.a: She laughed at her own mistake and praised his effort rather than neatness, showing that good enough is fine.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel handing over homework with a scratch-out?
qa.a: Vijay seems nervous and unsure, but also braver, trying out "good enough".

grounding: Shows over a week a parent torn between pride and worry who models her own mistakes and praises effort.

passage: Ojas, you get this from your father, you know. When Mohit was nine, he'd rewrite a whole essay if one letter leaned. I was so proud of his neat books, and so worried when he cried at midnight over a smudge. One night I did something I'd never done. I, Jyoti, showed him my old college file, full of red marks, and told him about the exam I failed and passed the next year. He couldn't believe his mother had ever failed. After that, when he fretted, I'd say, "Good enough is good enough, beta. Now sleep." I never told him to stop caring. Just to stop hurting. Now look at him. He still double-checks everything, but he sleeps.

qa.q: What did Jyoti show Mohit?
qa.a: Her old college file, full of red marks.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling about young Mohit's habits?
qa.a: She was proud of his neat books and worried when he cried at midnight over a smudge.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Jyoti sharing her own failed exam, which showed Mohit that mistakes can be survived.

qa.q: How might young Mohit have felt seeing his mother's red marks?
qa.a: Mohit was probably amazed and relieved, learning that even his mother had failed and recovered.

grounding: Shows a parent torn between pride and worry who shares her own failures and teaches good enough without shaming standards.

passage: The history project was due Monday, and on Saturday Damini still hadn't started. Every time she opened a blank document, her chest tightened: what if it wasn't the best in class, like last time? Then the power went out across the colony, and with it the laptop battery. By candlelight she panicked, writing and crossing out till two in the morning. On Monday she submitted it, exhausted. On Friday the result came: 19 out of 20, the highest in class. Her friend Sonali squealed and hugged her. Damini smiled for the photo, but on the walk home she felt nothing, only a flat, grey tiredness, and one thought: next time, it has to be 20.

qa.q: What mark did Damini get?
qa.a: 19 out of 20, the highest in class.

qa.q: How did Damini feel on the walk home?
qa.a: She felt empty and flat, with no joy, already raising the bar to 20.

qa.q: What could help Damini before the next project?
qa.a: Starting with a rough draft early and talking to a trusted adult about how the pressure feels.

qa.q: How might Sonali see Damini's result?
qa.a: Sonali is thrilled for her, not seeing the empty feeling behind Damini's smile.

grounding: Shows a teen who delays from dread, works late in a panic and feels empty after a top result as the standard rises.

passage: At the tuition centre in Hyderabad, Kishore got his mock board result: 96 in physics. Farida-ma'am read it out, and the class clapped. Kishore nodded and went back to his seat. Two months ago, 90 would have made him dance. Now he was already counting the four marks he'd lost. That night he sat at his desk from nine to two, not studying, just opening the chemistry book and closing it, too scared to begin in case he couldn't do it perfectly. At breakfast his little sister asked why he never played carrom any more. He didn't have an answer. He used to love chemistry. Now it felt like a test he was always about to fail.

qa.q: What did Kishore score in physics?
What was Kishore feeling when he kept opening and closing the chemistry book?
qa.a: He was scared of not doing it perfectly, so fear stopped him even starting.

qa.q: How could Farida-ma'am or his family help Kishore?
qa.a: Notice the pressure, talk with him about it, and help him rediscover enjoyment rather than only marks.

qa.q: What is it like for his little sister when Kishore stops playing carrom?
qa.a: She probably misses him and feels confused about why he has changed.

grounding: Illustrates a teen whose rising standards lead to late nights, dread-driven delay and loss of joy.

passage:
"You got the scholarship, Thomas! Why aren't you celebrating?"
"I don't know, Manoj. It felt good for about ten seconds."
"Ten seconds? I'd be dancing on the roof for a week."
"The next round is harder. If I don't get top ten there, what was the point of this one?"
"You've been saying that since Class 8. First it was the school prize, then the district, now this."
Thomas picked at the label on his water bottle. "I haven't even started the next essay. Every time I open it, I just can't."
"Because you don't know what to write?"
"Because what if it's not good enough."
Manoj was quiet. "Remember when we used to do science club stuff just for fun? You loved that."
"Yeah." Thomas looked out of the window. "I miss that."

qa.q: How long did the scholarship feel good for Thomas?
qa.a: About ten seconds.

qa.q: Why hasn't Thomas started the next essay?
qa.a: He is afraid it won't be good enough, so dread stops him beginning.

qa.q: What could Manoj suggest to help Thomas?
qa.a: Doing something just for fun again, and talking to a teacher or parent about the pressure.

qa.q: How does Manoj see Thomas's pattern?
qa.a: Manoj sees the goal keep moving since Class 8 and misses the old, fun-loving Thomas.

grounding: Shows a teen who feels little after success, delays from fear, and whose standards keep rising while joy fades.

passage:
Monday: When the maths marks came back, Akash had 98, the top score. Sarita, two benches behind, saw him stare at the two missing marks, jaw tight, and skip lunch to redo the sum.
Wednesday: Some boys muttered, "Show-off topper," as Akash passed. Sarita didn't join in. She told him, "That proof you did was really clean." He looked startled, then nodded.
Friday: Sarita asked if he wanted to come for pani puri after school with her and Rhea. He hesitated. "Just twenty minutes." He stayed an hour and laughed twice.

qa.q: What score did Akash get?
qa.a: 98, the top score.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when she saw Akash skip lunch?
qa.a: She felt concerned for him, noticing how anxious two lost marks made him.

qa.q: What did Sarita do that eased Akash's isolation?
qa.a: She refused to mock him, gave a specific compliment and invited him out to relax.

qa.q: What is it like for Akash to hear "Show-off topper"?
qa.a: Akash likely feels lonely and misunderstood, since his success brings pressure rather than joy.

grounding: Shows a classmate noticing a topper's anxiety, staying kind instead of mocking, and inviting him to relax.

passage: When I was fifteen, beta, there was a boy in my class called Raghav who topped every exam. Everyone disliked him a little for it. I did too, at first. Then one day he got 89 in biology, and I found him crying behind the chemistry lab, saying his father would ask about the eleven marks. I didn't know what to say. So I, Payal, who had got 61, sat next to him and said, "Eighty-nine is more than I'll ever get." He laughed, wet-faced. After that I stopped calling him "topper" and started inviting him to our Sunday cricket. He was terrible at it. He laughed more than I'd ever heard. We're still friends, you know. He's the uncle who brings you mangoes.

qa.q: What did Raghav get in biology?
What did young Payal feel on finding Raghav crying?
qa.a: Payal felt surprised and unsure what to say, and moved to comfort him instead of resenting him.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Payal sat with Raghav, then stopped calling him topper and invited him to Sunday cricket.

qa.q: How did Raghav experience being included in the cricket?
qa.a: He relaxed and laughed more than ever, feeling less alone despite being terrible at the game.

grounding: Shows a classmate who stops resenting a topper, notices his anxiety over marks and invites him to relax.

passage: The class-trip bus broke down on the ghat road in pouring rain, and everyone groaned, then started singing antakshari. Everyone except Harsha, the class topper, who sat at the back with a chemistry guide open on her knees, lips moving. Ira watched her for a while. Some boys joked that Harsha would study at her own wedding. Ira didn't laugh. She'd seen Harsha's hands shake last week when a test came back with one mark cut. Ira slid into the seat beside her. "We need one more for our team, and you know all the old songs." Harsha glanced at the book. "I have a test on Monday." "It'll still be there in ten minutes." Harsha closed it, slowly, and joined in on the second song.

qa.q: Where did the bus break down?
qa.a: On the ghat road, in pouring rain.

qa.q: What was Ira thinking as she watched Harsha study?
qa.a: Ira felt concerned, remembering Harsha's shaking hands over one lost mark, and didn't find the jokes funny.

qa.q: Why was Ira's invitation a good approach?
qa.a: It was kind and light, didn't mock Harsha's success and gave her a small, safe reason to relax.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel when she closes the book?
qa.a: Harsha may feel nervous about the test but relieved to be included and to take a break.

grounding: Illustrates a peer noticing a topper's anxiety, not mocking her success and inviting her to relax.

passage:
March: Gurpreet decided to apply for a design internship in Bengaluru. He opened the portfolio file, changed the font eleven times and closed it. "It has to be perfect, or they'll laugh," he told his sister, Gurleen.
April: The deadline passed. Gurpreet told everyone the internship wasn't worth it anyway. Secretly, he redid the cover page again.
May: Gurleen found a new deadline at a smaller studio and sat with him at the kitchen table. "Send the one you have. Not perfect. Just sent." His hands sweated over the button. He didn't press it that night. The next morning he did, and then felt sick for an hour.

qa.q: How many times did Gurpreet change the font?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet say the internship wasn't worth it?

qa.q: What helped Gurpreet finally send an application?

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel watching him hesitate over the button?
qa.a: Gurleen likely feels patient but worried, wanting him to stop missing chances.

grounding: Shows a young adult who delays applying because the work isn't flawless, missing a deadline before finally sending.

passage: You think I was always this quick with letters? At twenty, beta, I couldn't finish anything. A scholarship form for a Delhi college sat in my drawer for three months because my handwriting on page two wasn't neat enough. Either it would be perfect, or I wouldn't send it at all. I missed that deadline. And the next one. My friend Deepak finally sat with me on our veranda with a pen and a clock. "One hour. Whatever's on the page, we post it." I, Devika, wept over one crooked line. We posted it. I didn't get that scholarship. But I got the next one, and I've sent a lot of imperfect letters since. Imperfect things get finished. Perfect ones stay in drawers.

qa.q: How long did the form sit in the drawer?
qa.a: For three months.

qa.q: What did young Devika feel over the crooked line?
qa.a: Devika felt upset and afraid, as if one flaw made the whole form worthless.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Deepak sat with a pen and a clock and set one hour, so the form was finally posted.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt watching the tears over one line?
qa.a: Deepak was probably patient and a little worried, determined to help the form finally get posted.

grounding: Shows a young adult caught in all-or-nothing thinking who misses deadlines until someone helps finish an imperfect form.

passage: The job portal closed at midnight, the hostel Wi-Fi kept dropping, and Rukmini still hadn't sent a single application. For three weeks she'd been polishing one cover letter. Every draft had something wrong: a stiff sentence, a word used twice. "If it's not perfect, they'll bin it anyway," she told Nazia, her roommate, who had already sent fourteen. At eleven the Wi-Fi died completely. Rukmini sat on the floor, surrounded by printed drafts, and felt the familiar mix of panic and relief: now she couldn't send it, so she couldn't fail. Nazia offered her phone's data. Rukmini stared at it. "It's not ready," she said. The clock turned midnight. Nothing was sent.

qa.q: How many applications had Nazia sent?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Rukmini have when the Wi-Fi died?
qa.a: She felt panic and relief together, relieved that she couldn't send it and so couldn't fail.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could help next time?
qa.a: Waiting for a perfect letter meant nothing was sent; setting a time limit and sending a good-enough draft could help.

qa.q: What is it like for Nazia to offer her data and see it refused?
qa.a: Nazia may feel frustrated and worried for Rukmini, watching the deadline pass.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult whose all-or-nothing thinking leaves a job application unsent despite weeks of work.

passage:
Week one, a Tuesday: Kiran set a phone timer for forty-five minutes and wrote the ugliest first draft of an essay she'd ever allowed herself. When the alarm rang, she stopped, mid-sentence.
Week two, a Friday: Stuck again on one paragraph, she asked herself Aparna's question: what if this was only ninety percent of my best? Would anyone notice? She submitted it with one clumsy sentence left in. Her hands shook a little.
Week five, a Monday: The essay came back with a B-plus. Kiran felt a stab of disappointment, then relief. She told Aparna the worry still woke her at night, and that afternoon they booked a slot with the college counsellor.

qa.q: How long was Kiran's timer?
qa.a: Forty-five minutes.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when the B-plus came back?
qa.a: She felt a stab of disappointment, then relief.

qa.q: Which strategies helped Kiran finish?
qa.a: A time limit, a rough first draft and asking what ninety percent would look like, plus seeing a counsellor when the worry kept waking her.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel when Kiran shares that the worry still wakes her?
qa.a: Aparna likely feels concerned but glad Kiran is honest, and supportive in booking the counsellor.

grounding: Shows over weeks a young adult using time limits, rough drafts and a ninety-percent question, and seeking support for lasting worry.

passage: Gautam, sit. You remind me of myself at twenty, redrawing the same bridge plan till the paper went soft. My teacher at the polytechnic, old Mr Fernandes, took the pencil away. "One hour. Rough version. Then we see." I, Asif, argued. He tapped the clock. The rough version had mistakes, but it stood up. He asked me, "If this is ninety percent of your dream, will the bridge fall?" It wouldn't. So I started making small, deliberate imperfections: sending a letter with one typo, leaving a drawing a bit unfinished. It was agony at first. And when the worry kept me up for weeks, I spoke to a doctor. That was hard too, admitting I needed help. Now I finish things.

qa.q: Who took the pencil away?
qa.a: Old Mr Fernandes, the teacher at the polytechnic.

qa.q: What was young Asif feeling when asked to make a rough version?
qa.a: He felt resistant and anxious, arguing because anything less than perfect felt wrong.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Mr Fernandes's question about ninety percent, which showed the rough bridge would still stand.

qa.q: How might Mr Fernandes have seen young Asif's redrawing?
qa.a: He likely saw a talented student stuck on perfect and cared enough to set a firm time limit.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to set time limits, make rough versions, practise small imperfections and seek help for lasting worry.

passage: With three hours left before the film-club submission closed and the editing software crashing every twenty minutes, Amandeep made a decision she'd been practising for weeks. No more perfect cuts. She set a timer for ninety minutes and finished a rough version first, jumpy transition and all. "What if it's ninety percent as good as I want?" she asked her teammate Ujjwal. "Then it's better than a hundred percent of nothing," he said, handing her chai. She rendered it with one shaky shot still in. When she pressed submit, her stomach flipped, then settled. Later that week she admitted to Ujjwal that worry about her work kept her awake most nights, and he walked with her to the student wellbeing office.

qa.q: How long was Amandeep's timer?
qa.a: Ninety minutes.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when she pressed submit?
qa.a: Her stomach flipped with nerves, then settled into calm.

qa.q: Why was walking to the wellbeing office a wise step?
qa.a: Because her worry was keeping her awake most nights, which needs real support beyond tricks.

qa.q: What is it like for Ujjwal to hear about the sleepless nights?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably feels concerned and wants to help, so he walks with her.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult choosing good enough under pressure, finishing a rough version and seeking support for ongoing worry.

passage: At eleven at night, Shankar was still at his desk in the Chennai office, checking the client report for the fourth time. Karthik, his junior, had offered to do the charts, but Shankar had redone them anyway. "The colours were slightly off," he said, and Karthik's face fell. At home, his wife had kept dinner warm and gone to sleep. Their anniversary dinner last week had ended early because Shankar corrected the waiter twice and then criticised the dessert. He lay awake till three, running through the slide order, jaw aching. In the morning he snapped at Karthik about a comma. Karthik said nothing, but at lunch he quietly asked HR about moving teams.

qa.q: How many times had Shankar checked the client report?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What might Shankar be feeling as he lies awake till three?
qa.a: He is tense and exhausted, unable to let go of the worry that something isn't perfect.

qa.q: What could Shankar try, for his work and his relationships?
qa.a: Let Karthik's charts stand, check once and stop, and notice how his criticism is hurting people close to him.

qa.q: How does Karthik feel after his charts are redone and he is snapped at?
qa.a: Karthik feels discouraged and unvalued, enough to ask about leaving the team.

grounding: Shows a professional who rechecks everything, won't delegate and criticises others, with exhaustion and strained relationships as the cost.

passage:
"You're re-folding the towels I folded."
"They were uneven, Chandrika."
"They're towels, Mehak."
"If I don't fix it, it'll bother me all night." Mehak smoothed one edge. "Also, the dishes were stacked wrong."
"I used to love cooking with you. Now I don't want to do anything in this flat, because you'll redo it."
Mehak stopped. "That's not fair. I'm just... I do this at work too. I redid the whole team's presentation last night. I slept three hours."
"And how did your team feel?"
"Annoyed. My manager says I have to delegate or I'll burn out."
Chandrika sat on the bed. "Then practise here. Leave one towel wonky."
Mehak stared at it for a long time. Her hand twitched. She left it.

qa.q: How many hours did Mehak sleep after redoing the presentation?
qa.a: Three hours.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she left the towel wonky?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and tense, her hand twitching, but was trying to tolerate imperfection.

qa.q: What small practice did Chandrika suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Leaving one towel wonky, a safe way to practise imperfection before trying it at work.

qa.q: How does Chandrika feel living with Mehak's redoing?
qa.a: Chandrika feels discouraged and pushed out, no longer wanting to do anything in the flat.

grounding: Illustrates a professional whose rechecking and redoing strains home and work, with burnout close.

passage: Last Diwali I missed my own family lunch because I was re-checking a spreadsheet three people had already checked. I'm Pradeep, twenty-six, and I'm good at my job. Everybody says so. What they don't say, I've started noticing: my team stopped bringing me ideas. When Irfan, my closest colleague, gave me his draft last month, I covered it in red and called it "basically unusable". He hasn't eaten lunch with me since. My back aches all the time. I can't sleep before a deadline. The worst part is I talk to myself the same way: every tiny mistake, I call myself useless. I used to think that was just high standards. Now I think it's costing me people.

qa.q: What did Pradeep miss last Diwali?
qa.a: The family lunch.

qa.q: How does Pradeep feel about the cost of the perfectionism?
qa.a: Pradeep feels worn out and regretful, seeing it cost friendships and health.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do first to repair things with Irfan?
qa.a: Apologise for the harsh words and give specific, fair feedback, starting with what worked in the draft.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt when his draft was called unusable?
qa.a: Irfan was probably hurt and humiliated, which is why he stopped eating lunch with Pradeep.

grounding: Shows a professional who rechecks, criticises himself and others harshly, and sees the cost in burnout and lost closeness.

passage: Playground note, Class 3, Thursday. Omkar, new since his family moved in March, tried to run the whole tag game again. "You have to touch the tree, not the wall! And only I say when it starts!" When Shalini changed the base to the swings, he shouted, kicked the sand and walked off. I have noticed he does this most on days his mother is late for pickup. So I have started a fixed game-time routine for the class: same place, rules on a chart, one new rule allowed only on Fridays. Today he let Shalini's swing base stay, arms crossed but playing. Next step: I will invite him to help write Friday's new rule.

qa.q: Where did Shalini move the base?
qa.a: To the swings.

qa.q: What might Omkar be feeling when the base changes?
qa.a: He seems anxious and angry, since fixed rules help him feel safe after a big move.

qa.q: Which of the note-writer's steps is helping, and why?
qa.a: The fixed routine with rules on a chart, because predictable structure lets Omkar loosen his grip.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when Omkar kicks the sand and walks off?
qa.a: Shalini may feel confused or annoyed, since she only suggested a new base.

grounding: Shows a child who insists on fixed rules in games, with an adult using calm, predictable structure to help him loosen control.

passage:
Sunday. Dilnaz came over and wanted to play Ludo her way, where you don't need a six to start. That's NOT the rule. I told her, and she said it's more fun, and I said then go and play at your house. She went home. Now I feel bad. I don't know why I get so upset when rules change. It's like when Papa's job changed and we had to move and nothing was the same. At least in Ludo I know what happens. Mumma said tomorrow we can make a rule chart with Dilnaz: my rule on Monday, her rule on Tuesday. Maybe I can try hers once. Once.
Vasudha

qa.q: What was Dilnaz's rule for Ludo?
qa.a: You don't need a six to start.

qa.q: How does Vasudha feel after Dilnaz goes home?
qa.a: Vasudha feels bad and guilty, and confused about getting so upset over a changed rule.

passage: Behind the panchayat office in a village near Jhansi, Nikita drew the hopscotch squares with a stick and explained the rules, all nine of them, to Afreen and the Yadav twins. Stones must land exactly inside. No hopping on the lines. Nikita goes first. When Afreen suggested a double jump at the end, Nikita's face went red. "No! That's wrong!" She stamped on the squares, smudging them. Since her Baba had gone to work in the city, Nikita had been like this about everything: the same route to school, the same seat, the same rules. Her Dadi, watching from the charpai, called her over. "Same time every evening, you girls play here. Nikita's rules today. Afreen's one new rule tomorrow." Nikita chewed her lip, then nodded.

qa.q: How many rules did Nikita explain?
qa.a: All nine of them.

qa.q: What might Nikita be feeling when Afreen suggests a double jump?
qa.a: She seems anxious and angry, since fixed rules feel safe while her Baba is away.

qa.q: Why is Dadi's plan a good one?
qa.a: It gives a calm, predictable structure, with one new rule on a set day, so change feels manageable.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel when Nikita smudges the squares?
qa.a: Afreen likely feels startled and hurt that a small idea caused such anger.

grounding: Shows a child insisting on fixed game rules for safety during uncertainty, and an elder offering calm, predictable structure.

passage:
Rehana,
I owe you a proper apology, so I'm writing it. At the class picnic I planned everything: the bus, the food, who sat where, which games. When you suggested going to the lake instead of the fort, I said no before you'd finished. Then I corrected how you packed the sandwiches. In front of everyone. You went quiet the rest of the day, and I only understood why when Pooja said you felt like a passenger at your own picnic. The truth is, when I'm not in charge, my stomach ties itself in knots, as if something will go wrong and it will be my fault. That's my stuff, not yours. Next time, will you plan half? I'll try not to fix it.
Bhavna

qa.a: Rehana felt unheard, like a passenger at the picnic, and went quiet.

grounding: Shows a teen who takes over every plan and corrects others out of anxiety, leaving a friend feeling unheard.

passage: You want to know why I gave up the football captaincy? It wasn't the coach. It was me. I'm Omkar, Class 10, and I was the kind of captain who told everyone where to stand, how to kick, when to drink water. Rukmini, our goalkeeper, finally said in front of the whole team, "You never ask us anything." I was furious. Then I went home and couldn't sleep, because she was right. If I wasn't controlling every pass, I felt the whole match would fall apart and it would be my fault. That's fear, not leadership. So I gave the armband to her for a month. Hardest month of my life. We won two matches, lost one. I survived.

qa.q: Who said "You never ask us anything"?
qa.a: Rukmini, the goalkeeper.

qa.q: What was Omkar afraid of when not controlling every pass?
qa.a: Omkar feared the match would fall apart and it would be Omkar's fault.

qa.q: Which choice helped Omkar most, and why?
qa.a: Handing the armband to Rukmini for a month, which showed things could go on without total control.

qa.q: How might the team have felt under Omkar as captain?
qa.a: The team probably felt unheard and bossed around, since they were never asked for ideas.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who controls every play out of fear, leaves teammates unheard and tries letting someone else lead.

passage:
Tuesday night. Kunal and I planned the trip to Rishikesh, which really means I planned it and sent him a list of what to pack, when to leave, which auto to take. He laughed and said, "I've been travelling alone since I was sixteen, Shreya." I laughed too, but then I checked the train status four times and texted him twice to confirm he'd charged his phone. Why do I do this? I think if I don't hold every thread, something will snap and it'll be my fault. My counsellor said to try one small thing: let him book the hotel, and don't check the booking. I've written it here so I stick to it.
Shreya

qa.q: How many times did Shreya check the train status?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What is Shreya afraid of underneath the planning?
qa.a: Shreya fears something will snap and be Shreya's fault if every thread isn't held.

qa.q: What small step is Shreya trying, and why might it help?
qa.a: Letting Kunal book the hotel without checking, a small way to practise trust.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel getting a packing list?
qa.a: Kunal seems amused but may also feel slightly doubted, having travelled alone since sixteen.

grounding: Shows a young adult who micromanages a partner out of fear of things going wrong and practises trust in a small step.

passage: At the village feast in Saligao, Kunal had been at the youth group's cake stall since six, checking the price labels, re-stacking the plates, telling Elizabeth how to cut each slice. "Thinner. No, from the middle." When the bishop's visit was delayed and nobody knew when the crowd would come, Kunal paced between the tables, phone in hand, jaw tight. Elizabeth finally took the knife from him. "Kunal. Go and sit under the mango tree for fifteen minutes. I'll run it. If something goes wrong, we fix it." He wanted to argue. Instead he went, and sat, and watched from a distance as she cut the slices thicker than he would have. People bought them anyway. His shoulders came down, a little.

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth send Kunal?
qa.a: To sit under the mango tree for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when nobody knew when the crowd would come?
qa.a: He felt anxious and tense, pacing with his jaw tight because the uncertainty felt unsafe.

qa.q: Why was Elizabeth's suggestion helpful?
qa.a: It gave Kunal a short, safe chance to trust someone else and see the stall run fine without him.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel being told exactly how to cut each slice?
qa.a: Elizabeth likely feels a bit irritated and doubted, which is why she takes the knife.

grounding: Shows a young adult micromanaging out of anxiety about uncertainty, then practising trust by stepping back.
